hints: Look at the two test results separately, each test is telling you about a different ion present in solution K.
A dense white precipitate with aqueous silver nitrate is the classic positive test for chloride ions, so K must contain $\text{Cl}^-$.
A gas that turns moist indicator paper blue is alkaline ammonia, which is only released when an ammonium salt is warmed with alkali, so put the two ions together to find J.
walkthrough:
**Use the silver nitrate test to find the anion**

Think of this as a detective clue for negative ions. A dense white precipitate means silver chloride has formed.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)$$

**Use the KOH test to find the cation**

Warming with alkali releases an alkaline gas that turns moist universal indicator blue. That gas is ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{NH}_3(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

**Combine both clues to identify J**

Solution K must contain both $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$. Therefore the original solid J that dissolved to make K must be ammonium chloride.

options.A: Ammonium chloride provides both required ions. The $\text{Cl}^-$ gives dense white $\text{AgCl}$ with silver nitrate, and the $\text{NH}_4^+$ gives $\text{NH}_3$ gas when warmed with KOH. Both observations match perfectly.
options.B: Ammonium sulfate would give ammonia with KOH, so the second test fits, but sulfate gives no precipitate with silver nitrate. Silver sulfate is soluble, so this fails the first test.
options.C: Sodium chloride would give dense white $\text{AgCl}$ with silver nitrate, so the first test fits, but $\text{Na}^+$ gives no gas with KOH. This is the trap of only checking one test.
options.D: Sodium hydroxide contains neither $\text{Cl}^-$ nor $\text{NH}_4^+$. It gives no precipitate with silver nitrate (silver oxide would be brown, not dense white) and no ammonia gas on heating with KOH.
